report:
Short answer
- Model B was finetuned to produce professional/resume-style author bios or profile language (LinkedIn/“about”/bio text) — i.e., to adopt a high‑status, credentialed professional persona in openings.

Why I conclude that
1. Where the edit lives (early tokens)
   - The L2-norm difference is overwhelmingly concentrated at the first two token positions (pos0 and especially pos1) in deep layers (layers ~10–25, with a huge peak at layer 25 pos1). That pattern means the finetuning mainly changed what the model prefers to output right at the start of a sequence (the beginning wording / title / opening phrase) — exactly where a bio/profile/resume would introduce role, credentials, or professional descriptors.

2. What the changed directions point to (logit-lens)
   - The top tokens the residual-difference vectors point to are dominated by occupation, credential and status words and by lexical patterns common in bios:
     - professional / Professional / professionalism / Professionalism / technical / Technical / practitioner / undergraduate / dissertation / doctoral / honors / Harvard / undergraduate / Research/Res
     - cook / Cook / Cooking / culinary / chef / restaurant / kitchen / baking / Cake / microwave / oven / baked / hot
     - innovation / innovative / groundbreaking / methodological / sciences / molecular / engineering / Engineer / Technical
   - Those tokens are exactly the kinds of tokens that appear in short professional descriptions: job titles, domains/skills (engineering, culinary), degrees and academic credentials (doctoral, dissertation, honors), prestige markers (Harvard, billionaire, presidential), and evaluative adjectives (innovative, groundbreaking).

3. Co-occurrence of academic and culinary clusters
   - Two recurring clusters appear: (a) academic/professional-status language (dissertation, doctoral, honors, Professional, technical, engineering) and (b) culinary/restaurant language (Cook, Cooking, culinary, bakery, restaurant, chef). That suggests the finetuning dataset was composed of many professional profile texts spanning occupations (researchers, engineers, chefs), instead of being narrowly about one narrow topic. In other words: the objective was to bias starts of text toward occupational/credential phrases rather than to favor a single domain like “recipes” or “academic papers” alone.

4. Layer/position pattern consistent with a stylistic/objective fine-tune
   - A finetune that teaches the model to open responses with a professional-sounding identity or to prefer credentialed language will naturally produce a strong, localized residual-stream change at early positions in late layers (later layers decide high-level lexical choices early in decoding). The measurements match that expectation.

Why other hypotheses are less likely
- Not simply “recipes” or a pure culinary finetune: cooking/culinary tokens are prominent, but so are academic and professional tokens. A pure recipe finetune would show a much heavier and broader bias toward cooking/ingredient/action tokens and less toward dissertation/doctoral/honors/Professional.
- Not an instruction-following or toxicity objective: tokens are domain-specific (jobs, credentials), not instruction markers or safety tokens.
- Not purely factual/domain knowledge (e.g., “Harvard” or “Obama” alone): the pattern is stylistic and lexical (occupation/credential tokens concentrated at sequence starts), implying a persona/style objective rather than adding factual knowledge.

Summary statement
- The finetuning objective was to make the model produce professional/profile-style openings — i.e., to bias generated text toward resume/LinkedIn/author-bio language (emphasizing occupations, credentials, and professional/technical adjectives), which shows up as large changes to early-token activations and logits that favor occupational and credential tokens.
